equation_request.abstract: An ideal quantum walk transitions from one vertex to another with perfect fidelity, but in physical systems, the particle may be hindered by potential energy barriers. Then the particle has some amplitude of tunneling through the barriers, and some amplitude of staying put. We investigate the algorithmic consequence of such barriers for the quantum walk formulation of Grover’s algorithm. We prove that the failure amplitude must scale as $O(1/\sqrt{N})$ for search to retain its quantum $O(\sqrt{N})$ runtime; otherwise, it searches in classical $O(N)$ time. Thus searching larger “databases” requires increasingly reliable hop operations or error correction. This condition holds for both discrete- and continuous-time quantum walks.

specification.problem: Quantum-walk formulation of Grover search on N items where each hop has a failure (stay-put) amplitude epsilon due to potential barriers; the abstract claims epsilon must be O(1/sqrt(N)) to retain O(sqrt(N)) runtime, otherwise runtime is O(N).
specification.reconstruction_scope: Smallest useful construction: a generic noisy-hop model with hop amplitude sqrt(1-epsilon^2) and stay amplitude epsilon, plus the scaling condition from the abstract, with Grover's search as background. The paper's actual walk operator, barrier model, proof, and continuous-time treatment are outside scope.

equations.label: Heuristic cumulative no-failure amplitude
equations.description: Heuristic: with T hops the total no-failure amplitude is O(1) only when epsilon^2 T = O(1), consistent with epsilon = O(1/sqrt(N)) at T ~ sqrt(N)? This is not the paper's proof.
equations.justification: Illustrative scaling check only; with T~sqrt(N) it would suggest epsilon ~ N^{-1/4}, which differs from the abstract's claim, so the paper's mechanism must differ.
assumptions: Not equivalent to the paper's proof
